oneLiner: What you pay for each ₹1 the company earns.

byLevel.new: P/E means price-to-earnings. At a P/E of 28.4, investors are paying ₹28.40 for every ₹1 the company earns in a year. A high number can mean people expect strong growth — or that the stock is simply expensive.
byLevel.learning: A P/E well above the sector median means the market expects this company to grow faster than its peers. That expectation has to be met.
byLevel.practicing: P/E relative to sector median is the comparison that matters, not the absolute number.
byLevel.independent: P/E vs sector median.

oneLiner: Profit earned per share over the last year.

byLevel.new: EPS means earnings per share — the company's profit divided by the number of shares. It tells you how much profit sits behind each share you own.
byLevel.learning: EPS growth matters more than the absolute figure. Rising EPS is what justifies a rising price.
byLevel.practicing: Track EPS growth against price growth.
byLevel.independent: EPS trend.

oneLiner: News everyone already knows is usually already reflected in the price.

byLevel.new: 'Priced in' means the market already knows something, so the price has already moved. If a budget increase was announced months ago and everyone read it, buying today doesn't get you the surprise — you're paying a price that already includes the good news.
byLevel.learning: Public news is usually priced in. Ask what would be new information from here.
byLevel.practicing: Ask what is not yet priced in — that is where the edge would have to come from.
byLevel.independent: Largely priced in.

oneLiner: Work the company has already won but not yet delivered.

byLevel.new: An order book is work a company has won but has not delivered yet. Orders can be delayed or cancelled, so it does not guarantee revenue.
byLevel.learning: An order book gives possible future work, but timing, delivery, and cancellations affect conversion.
byLevel.practicing: Assess order-book value alongside conversion rate, timing, and cancellation history.
byLevel.independent: Order book conversion.

oneLiner: How much the company has borrowed compared with shareholders' equity.

byLevel.new: Debt to equity compares what a company has borrowed with shareholders' equity, the owners' accounting claim. A low number means it relies less on borrowed money, though context still matters.
byLevel.learning: Compare debt to equity against the sector — what counts as high differs by industry.
byLevel.practicing: D/E vs sector median; check interest coverage too.
byLevel.independent: D/E vs sector.

oneLiner: The highest and lowest price over the past year.

byLevel.new: The 52-week range is the highest and lowest the share has traded in the past year. Being near the high doesn't automatically mean expensive, and near the low doesn't mean cheap — you still have to check the business.
byLevel.learning: Position in the 52-week range is context, not a signal on its own.
byLevel.practicing: Range position tells you about sentiment, not value.
byLevel.independent: Range position.

oneLiner: Whether the price is reasonable for what the company earns.

byLevel.new: Valuation is about whether the price makes sense for what the company actually earns and owns. A good company can still be a bad buy if you pay too much for it.
byLevel.learning: Valuation is always relative — to peers, to the sector, and to the company's own history.
byLevel.practicing: Compare against peers and own history simultaneously.
byLevel.independent: Relative valuation.

oneLiner: An unofficial, unregulated price quoted before listing.

byLevel.new: GMP is the grey market premium — an unofficial price some dealers quote before a share is listed. It is not an exchange price, nobody regulates it, and it can change a lot in days. It reflects demand for the allotment, not whether the company is any good.
byLevel.learning: GMP measures short-term allotment demand, not business quality, and it is unregulated.
byLevel.practicing: GMP is an unregulated demand signal, not a valuation input.
byLevel.independent: GMP: unregulated demand signal.

oneLiner: The market value of all outstanding shares.

byLevel.new: Share price multiplied by the number of shares describes a company's market size.
byLevel.learning: Market cap groups companies by size but does not measure quality.
byLevel.practicing: Compare market cap with revenue, profit, and peers.
byLevel.independent: Market cap: price times shares.

oneLiner: Income recognized from selling products or services.

byLevel.new: Revenue is income recognized from sales or services before subtracting costs; it is not necessarily cash collected immediately.
byLevel.learning: Revenue growth shows whether sales are expanding or shrinking.
byLevel.practicing: Check growth over several periods and against the industry.
byLevel.independent: Revenue: top-line sales.

oneLiner: The share of revenue left as profit.

byLevel.new: A 10% margin means ₹10 profit for every ₹100 of revenue.
byLevel.learning: Margins show how efficiently sales become profit.
byLevel.practicing: Compare margins with history and similar businesses.
byLevel.independent: Profit margin: profit divided by revenue.

oneLiner: Profit from normal operations as a share of revenue.

byLevel.new: It shows what remains after everyday business costs, before interest and taxes.
byLevel.learning: It focuses on the core business rather than financing.
byLevel.practicing: Watch whether operating margins are stable or changing.
byLevel.independent: Operating margin: operating profit divided by revenue.

oneLiner: Cash moving into and out of a business.

byLevel.new: Cash flow tracks actual money received and paid, which can differ from accounting profit.
byLevel.learning: Operating cash flow shows whether normal activities generate cash.
byLevel.practicing: Compare operating cash flow with profit over time.
byLevel.independent: Operating cash flow: cash from core operations.

oneLiner: Cash left after maintaining and expanding the business.

byLevel.new: It is usually operating cash flow minus spending on property and equipment.
byLevel.learning: It indicates cash available after essential investment.
byLevel.practicing: Look for a repeatable trend, not one unusual period.
byLevel.independent: FCF: operating cash flow less capital expenditure.

oneLiner: Money spent on long-lived assets.

byLevel.new: Capex pays for assets such as equipment or buildings that help for years.
byLevel.learning: Capex can support growth but reduces cash when paid.
byLevel.practicing: Read capex with depreciation and operating cash flow.
byLevel.independent: Capex: investment in long-lived operating assets.

oneLiner: Profit earned for each unit of shareholder equity.

byLevel.new: ROE compares profit with shareholders' equity, the accounting value of their ownership claim in the company.
byLevel.learning: Debt can raise ROE, so read it with leverage measures.
byLevel.practicing: Compare ROE with peers and inspect what drives changes.
byLevel.independent: ROE: net income divided by average equity.

oneLiner: Operating profit earned from capital used in the business.

byLevel.new: ROCE asks how efficiently a business uses shareholder money and long-term borrowing.
byLevel.learning: It helps compare businesses using different amounts of debt.
byLevel.practicing: Compare ROCE with its history and cost of capital.
byLevel.independent: ROCE: operating profit relative to capital employed.

oneLiner: How comfortably operating profit can pay interest costs.

byLevel.new: It compares operating profit with interest a company must pay.
byLevel.learning: A larger ratio generally means more room for interest bills.
byLevel.practicing: Check stability and what happens when profit falls.
byLevel.independent: Interest coverage: EBIT divided by interest expense.

oneLiner: Annual dividend per share compared with share price.

byLevel.new: Yield estimates annual dividends as a percentage of the current share price.
byLevel.learning: Yield changes when either the dividend or price changes.
byLevel.practicing: Review payout history and cash generation, not yield alone.
byLevel.independent: Dividend yield: annual dividend divided by price.

oneLiner: The portion of profit paid as dividends.

byLevel.new: A 40% payout means ₹40 of every ₹100 profit is paid as dividends.
byLevel.learning: One-off profits can distort the ratio.
byLevel.practicing: Compare payout with cash flow and dividend history.
byLevel.independent: Payout ratio: dividends divided by net income.

oneLiner: Accounting value of assets minus liabilities.

byLevel.new: It is what the balance sheet says remains after subtracting liabilities from assets.
byLevel.learning: Book value may differ from economic value, especially for brands.
byLevel.practicing: Use it with sector and accounting context.
byLevel.independent: Book value: assets less liabilities.

oneLiner: Share price compared with book value per share.

byLevel.new: P/B compares what the market pays for a share with its accounting value.
byLevel.learning: It is often more useful for asset-heavy businesses.
byLevel.practicing: Compare it with peers and company history.
byLevel.independent: P/B: price divided by book value per share.

oneLiner: A company value measure including debt and subtracting cash.

byLevel.new: EV starts with equity value, adds debt, and subtracts cash.
byLevel.learning: It helps compare companies with different debt and cash.
byLevel.practicing: Pair EV with an operating measure and check adjustments.
byLevel.independent: EV: equity value plus debt minus cash.

oneLiner: Operating earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization.

byLevel.new: EBITDA is a simplified view of operating earnings before financing, taxes, and certain non-cash charges.
byLevel.learning: It is not cash flow because it ignores working capital and capital spending.
byLevel.practicing: Reconcile EBITDA with reported profit and cash flow.
byLevel.independent: EBITDA: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization.

oneLiner: How widely and quickly a price has moved.

byLevel.new: Volatility describes how much prices fluctuate; higher means larger or more frequent moves.
byLevel.learning: Historical volatility describes past movement, not a guaranteed future move.
byLevel.practicing: Compare matching periods and note major events.
byLevel.independent: Volatility: dispersion of price returns.

oneLiner: The last price recorded when the market closed on the previous trading day.

byLevel.new: It gives you yesterday's final market price to compare with today's price.
byLevel.learning: Comparing it with the current price shows the day's price change.
byLevel.practicing: Use it as a short-term reference, not a measure of business performance.
byLevel.independent: Previous close: the final traded price from the preceding session.
